etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English siȝht, siȝt, siht, from Old English siht, sihþ (“something seen; vision”), from Proto-West Germanic *sihti, equivalent to see +‎ -th. Cognate with Scots sicht, Saterland Frisian Sicht, West Frisian sicht, Dutch zicht, German Low German Sicht, German Sicht, Danish sigte, Swedish sikte.

definitions.definition: (in the singular) The ability to see.

quote.citation: c. 1588–1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: Thy sight is young, / And thou shalt read when mine begin to dazzle.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 12, line 67:
quote.text: O loſs of ſight, of thee I moſt complain!

definitions.definition: The act of seeing; perception of objects by the eye; view.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 1:9:
quote.text: And when hee had spoken these things, while they beheld, hee was taken vp, and a cloud receiued him out of their sight.

quote.citation: 2005, Plato, translated by Lesley Brown, Sophist, page 236d:
quote.text: He's a really remarkable man and it's very hard to get him in one's sights;  […]

definitions.definition: (often in the plural) Something worth seeing; a spectacle, either good or bad.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 3:3:
quote.text: And Moses saide, I will nowe turne aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.
They never saw a sight so fair.

definitions.definition: (often in the plural) A device used in aiming a projectile, through which the person aiming looks at the intended target.
A small aperture through which objects are to be seen, and by which their direction is settled or ascertained.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: their eyes of fire sparking through sights of steel

definitions.definition: (now colloquial) a great deal, a lot; frequently used to intensify a comparative.

quote.citation: 1913, D[avid] H[erbert] Lawrence, chapter 2, in Sons and Lovers, London: Duckworth & Co. […], →OCLC:
quote.text: "If your mother put you in the pit at twelve, it's no reason why I should do the same with my lad.""Twelve! It wor a sight afore that!"

definitions.definition: In a drawing, picture, etc., that part of the surface, as of paper or canvas, which is within the frame or the border or margin. In a frame, the open space, the opening.
(obsolete) The instrument of seeing; the eye.

quote.citation: c. 1607–1608, William Shakeſpeare, The Late, And much admired Play, Called Pericles, Prince of Tyre. […], London: Imprinted at London for Henry Goſſon,  […], published 1609, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: Why cloude they not their ſights perpetually,

quote.citation: 1720, William Wake, Principles of the Christian Religion in a Commentary on the Church Catechism:
quote.text: a very heinous Sin in the Sight of God

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 16:15:
quote.text: That which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To observe through, or as if through, a sight, to check the elevation, direction, levelness, or other characteristics of, especially when surveying or navigating.

quote.citation: 1912, John Herbert Farrell, Alfred Joseph Moses, Practical Field Geology, page 30:
quote.text: Next a point of known elevation, preferably one of the triangulation stations, is sighted; the vertical angle is read and the horizontal distance is scaled from the point of the setup on the map to the point sighted.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To see; to get sight of (something); to register visually.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter IV, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I was on my way to the door, but all at once, through the fog in my head, I began to sight one reef that I hadn't paid any attention to afore.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To apply sights to; to adjust the sights of.
(transitive, intransitive) To observe or aim (at something) using a (gun) sight.

quote.citation: 2005 August 2, C. J. Cherryh, The Deep Beyond, Penguin, →ISBN:
quote.text: Jim braced the gun and sighted, tried to pull the trigger. Beside him a body collapsed, limp. It was Max. A shot had gone through his brain. Jim stared down at him, numb with horror.

quote.citation: 2009, James Wright, FBI: Fidelity, Bravery, Integrity : an Autobiography, iUniverse, →ISBN, page 27:
quote.text: So I sighted the deer with my .30—30 and fired at him. The bullet hit about ten yards below the deer. I realized that I had a problem with the gun so I aimed about ten yards above the deer as he was running and he dropped dead on the [spot].

quote.citation: 2010 October 6, Bryce M. Towsley, Gunsmithing Made Easy: Projects for the Home Gunsmith, Skyhorse Publishing Inc., →ISBN:
quote.text: This buck was finally mine. I had spent hours shooting at moving targets with that rifle and there was no way I could miss. I raised my gun and sighted through the scope.
